summary:
We developed an integrated AI-powered health monitoring system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It combines an ESP32-based wearable device that monitors vital signs, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), body temperature, and ECG, with an AI-powered web platform that analyzes health data and interacts with astronauts.

Our system addresses three key health risks identified by NASA's Human Research Program: psychological health, sleep, and physical fitness. It monitors sleep patterns through physiological data, tracks exercise schedules, and uses interactive questionnaires and voice check-ins to identify potential indicators of psychological distress, social isolation, or depression. Based on these insights, the AI suggests personalized coping strategies inspired by NASA recommendations, such as spending time near a window, growing plants, and journaling.

This solution is particularly important for long-duration missions to Mars, where isolation, sleep disruption, and physical deterioration threaten crew health. Its autonomous monitoring and early risk identification aim to reduce dependence on real-time support from Earth.

**Project Repository:** [GitHub – NASA Project 2026](https://github.com/Samspei01/NASA-project-2026/tree/main)

The repository includes the complete project documentation, README, source code, system design, architecture diagrams, and hardware diagrams.
details:
MessiSat

Team To Space

1. The Problem

Long-term isolation increases the risk of anxiety and depression. During a Mars mission, communication with Earth will be delayed, making immediate psychological support difficult.

Disrupted light-dark cycles can negatively affect sleep and mission performance. Microgravity also weakens muscles, bones, and the cardiovascular system. This is why astronauts aboard the ISS exercise for approximately 1.5 hours daily.

Microgravity can also cause changes in the heart and blood vessels. Astronauts therefore need an integrated monitoring system that can track their health and provide timely warnings without depending on communication with Earth.

2. Our Strategy

We used NASA's Human Research Program (HRP) risk pages as the scientific foundation for our system.

Each identified risk was translated into a dedicated system module:

  • Behavioral and Psychiatric Risks: AI-powered mental health monitoring.
  • Sleep Risks: Sleep tracking and sleep-quality estimation.
  • Fitness Risks: Exercise monitoring and muscle-condition tracking.
  • Cardiovascular Risks: Heart rate, blood oxygen, and ECG monitoring.

This approach ensures that every system component addresses a specific challenge astronauts may face during long-duration space missions.

3. Hardware

We designed a custom PCB using EasyEDA, built around an ESP32 microcontroller.

The system integrates the following sensors:

  • MAX30102: Heart rate and blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) monitoring.
  • NTC Thermistor + ADS1115: Body temperature monitoring.
  • AD8232: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signal acquisition.

The firmware is written in C. The ESP32 collects sensor readings, processes the data, and transmits them over Wi-Fi to the web platform for visualization, storage, and analysis.

4. Web Platform (HTML, CSS, JavaScript)

The web platform provides a centralized interface for monitoring astronaut health.

Astronaut Profile

Stores essential information, including age, sex, and previous medical conditions, allowing health readings to be interpreted in context.

Live Vital Signs

Displays real-time health measurements, including:

  • Heart rate.
  • Blood oxygen saturation (SpO2).
  • Body temperature.
  • Heart-rate indicators.

Measurements update while the monitoring device is connected.

Data Logging

Records vital-sign readings at regular intervals for continuous health tracking.

Data-sharing permissions are designed according to privacy requirements:

  • Vital-sign data can be accessed by the astronaut, ground crew, and onboard medical staff.
  • Mental health results are shared only between the astronaut and the doctor to protect psychological privacy.

Alerts

Generates warnings whenever a monitored reading moves outside its predefined safe range.

Health Reports

Provides a consolidated report containing the astronaut's health measurements, monitoring history, and system results.

5. Mental Health AI

Long-term isolation is one of the major psychological challenges of deep-space missions.

To address this risk, we developed an AI-powered assistant using a Large Language Model (LLM) through an API, guided by a custom system prompt.

The assistant interacts with the astronaut and analyzes multiple sources of information:

  • Conversational Analysis: Examines the astronaut's messages for potential signs of psychological distress.
  • Questionnaires: Uses a combination of an established screening questionnaire and additional questions developed by our team.
  • Voice Analysis: Considers vocal tone as another potential indicator of emotional state.

The system screens for potential signs of depression.

When concerning indicators are identified, it suggests countermeasures inspired by NASA recommendations, such as:

  • Looking out of a window.
  • Growing plants.
  • Maintaining a personal journal.

The AI is designed as an early screening and support tool, not as a replacement for professional psychological assessment or medical diagnosis.

6. Sleep Monitoring

Sleep patterns can be significantly affected by artificial lighting, disrupted circadian rhythms, and the unusual schedules associated with space missions.

Our system uses heart-rate patterns to estimate whether the astronaut is asleep and evaluate potential changes in sleep quality.

By tracking these patterns over time, the platform aims to identify sleep disturbances and provide insights into the astronaut's sleeping habits.

7. Exercise and Muscle Monitoring

Physical activity is essential for preventing muscle deterioration during long-duration space missions.

Our system incorporates an AI-assisted exercise monitoring module that:

  • Follows a periodic exercise schedule.
  • Uses recorded vital signs during training to evaluate exercise performance.
  • Tracks estimated changes in muscle condition over time.

The platform displays a muscle-condition trend:

  • Stable: When the astronaut maintains the scheduled exercise routine.
  • Declining: When exercise is consistently missed or insufficient.

These muscle and bone indicators are estimates used for trend visualization in our prototype, not direct physiological measurements.

8. Heart and Blood Vessel Monitoring

Microgravity can affect cardiovascular function and blood circulation.

Our system monitors:

  • Heart Rate: Tracks changes in cardiovascular activity.
  • SpO2: Monitors blood oxygen saturation.
  • ECG: Records the heart's electrical activity.

These measurements help provide an overview of the astronaut's cardiovascular condition.

Researchers are still investigating why some astronauts experience changes in venous blood flow during spaceflight.

Our device is intended to complement existing health-monitoring procedures. It does not diagnose cardiovascular diseases or detect blood clots.

9. Testing and Limitations

The system uses actual sensor readings collected through our custom hardware.

However, certain scenarios, including illness-related conditions and depression cases, are simulated because proper validation requires additional time, participants, and clinical resources.

Current limitations include:

  • The prototype is not clinically validated.
  • Mental health results are screening indicators, not diagnoses.
  • Sleep quality is estimated using heart-rate patterns.
  • Muscle and bone conditions are represented through estimated trends rather than direct measurements.
  • The device does not replace professional medical equipment or clinical assessment.

MessiSat is a research prototype demonstrating how integrated hardware, AI, and web technologies could support astronaut health monitoring during long-duration space missions.

10. Future Work: AI Development

Our future development focuses on making the system more intelligent, personalized, and autonomous.

1. Personal Health Baselines

Develop AI models that learn each astronaut's normal physiological patterns and detect unusual deviations instead of relying entirely on fixed thresholds.

2. Predictive Health Warnings

Use historical health data to forecast potential sleep deterioration and increasing stress levels before they become more serious.

3. Onboard AI

Deploy lightweight AI models directly on the onboard hardware or local computing infrastructure, allowing the system to operate independently when communication with Earth is unavailable.

4. Circadian Lighting Coach

Develop an AI module that recommends or automatically adjusts cabin lighting schedules to support healthy sleep-wake cycles.

This concept builds on existing ISS LED lighting systems designed to simulate Earth's natural light cycle.

5. Adaptive Exercise Coach

Create an intelligent exercise assistant that dynamically adjusts workout schedules and intensity based on the astronaut's activity and estimated muscle-condition trends.

6. Virtual Nature

Generate AI-powered calming natural environments and interactive visual scenes that simulate the experience of looking through a window when a real external view is unavailable.

7. Explainable AI Alerts

Make AI-generated alerts more transparent by providing doctors with clear explanations of:

  • What abnormal pattern was detected.
  • Which measurements contributed to the alert.
  • Why the system considers the pattern concerning.

8. Real-World Validation

Conduct testing with real volunteers and collaborate with medical and research institutions to evaluate sensor accuracy, AI performance, and the reliability of the overall system.
dataRefs: The data generated by our device can be used to monitor the human body in a zero-gravity environment.
